content: Cephradine, also known as cefradine (INN), is a first-generation cephalosporin antibiotic. It is structurally and functionally similar to cephalexin and is used to treat a variety of bacterial infections. Cephradine is effective in treating infections such as tonsillitis, pharyngitis, and lobar pneumonia caused by Group A beta-hemolytic streptococci and Streptococcus pneumoniae (formerly Diplococcus pneumoniae). While penicillin remains the preferred drug for treating and preventing streptococcal infections, including the prophylaxis of rheumatic fever, cephradine (marketed as Velosef) is generally effective in eradicating streptococci from the nasopharynx. However, there is insufficient evidence to confirm its efficacy in preventing rheumatic fever. Cephradine is also indicated for the treatment of otitis media caused by Group A beta-hemolytic streptococci, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and staphylococci. Additionally, it is used to manage skin and skin structure infections caused by staphylococci (both penicillin-susceptible and penicillin-resistant strains) and beta-hemolytic streptococci. For urinary tract infections (UTIs), including prostatitis, cephradine is effective against Escherichia coli, Proteus mirabilis, Klebsiella species, and enterococci (Streptococcus faecalis). The high concentrations of cephradine achievable in the urinary tract make it effective against many strains of enterococci, even those that may show relative resistance in disc susceptibility studies. However, it is important to note that among beta-lactam antibiotics, ampicillin is the drug of choice for enterococcal urinary tract infections caused by E. faecalis. Cephradine is available in several formulations, including capsules containing 250 mg or 500 mg, syrup containing 250 mg/5 mL, and vials for injection containing 500 mg or 1 g.
